## References

1. [SWE-smith: Scaling Data for Software Engineering Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21798)

# Notes

**Authors:** John Yang, Kilian Lieret, Carlos E. Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kabir Khandpur, Yanzhe Zhang, Binyuan Hui, Ofir Press, Ludwig Schmidt, Diyi Yang (Stanford, Princeton, Alibaba Qwen). This is the SWE-bench / SWE-agent group, so this paper is written by the people who built the benchmark it trains for. Everything is open: toolkit, 50k tasks, trajectories, model (swesmith.com). v2, May 2025.

---

## 1. The problem: you can't train a SWE agent without executable tasks

A software-engineering (SWE) agent reads a GitHub issue, explores a repo, edits code, and runs tests. To *train* one (not just prompt one), you need many examples of the form:

> repo snapshot + issue text + a working execution environment + tests that tell you whether a fix is right.

The tests are the key ingredient. Without them you can only learn from what code *looks* like (imitating diffs) or from string-similarity rewards (does the patch resemble the gold patch). With them, you can run a strong model on a task, keep only the runs whose patch actually makes the tests pass, and train on those. That's the whole rejection-sampling recipe, and it depends entirely on having lots of executable tasks.

Before this paper, the open data situation was thin:

| Dataset | Tasks | Repos | Executable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| R2E | 0.25k | 137 | Yes (synthetic) |
| SWE-bench-train | 19k | 37 | No |
| SWE-fixer | 115k | 856 | No |
| SWE-gym | 2.4k | 11 | Yes |
| R2E-gym (subset) | 4.6k | 10 | Yes (synthetic) |
| SWE-bench-extra | 6.38k | 2k | Yes |
| **SWE-smith** | **50k** | **128** | **Yes (both real + synthetic)** |

Prior executable datasets need hundreds of GB to several TB of environment images; SWE-smith's 50k tasks fit in 295 GB.

The executable datasets topped out at a few thousand tasks from about ten repos. The reason is how SWE-bench-style collection works:

1. Crawl PRs. Keep only those that (a) link to an issue, (b) change code, and (c) add or modify tests. Very few PRs pass all three.
2. For each surviving PR, check out its *base commit* (the repo as it was when the PR was opened) and build an environment for *that version*. Old versions have old dependencies, so a human has to write version-specific install specs.
3. One Docker image per task instance, which is where the terabytes come from.

Their flask case study (Appendix C.2) puts numbers on it. SWE-bench got **11** flask tasks out of 2,434 PRs (0.45%). Only 107 had a linked issue plus new tests, and environments could be built for just 11 of those. That took about **38 human-hours**, or **~207 minutes per task**. SWE-smith on the same repo: 10 minutes to write install specs, 23 minutes of LM bug generation ($2.47), 14 minutes of validation → **267 tasks** at about **10.6 seconds and $0.006 each**.

---

## 2. The core idea: build the environment first, then break the code

The whole method follows from one inversion:

- **SWE-bench:** find a task (a real PR) → try to build an environment for it.
- **SWE-smith:** build *one* environment for a repo (latest commit, tests passing) → create many tasks *inside* it by breaking the code.

The key insight they state: **execution-based validation can do two jobs.** In SWE-bench, running tests checks whether a *solution* is right. In SWE-smith, running tests also checks whether a *bug* is real. A candidate bug counts only if it makes at least one previously passing test fail. That turns the test suite into a free filter for "is this a meaningful regression?"

Plain version: take a healthy codebase with good tests. Break it in many ways. Keep every break that a test catches. Each kept break, reversed, is a training task: "here's a bug report, fix it." The gold fix is simply the inverse of the bug patch.

Because all tasks from a repo share one Docker image, storage drops from an estimated 50-150 TB (if you built 50k SWE-bench-style per-task images) to 295 GB, roughly **500x less**.

---

## 3. The pipeline, stage by stage

### 3.1 Environment construction (mostly automated)

- **Repo choice:** start from the 5,000 most-downloaded PyPI packages (as of Nov 18, 2024). Sort by GitHub stars, drop anything under 1,000 stars, and drop the 12 SWE-bench test repos to avoid contaminating the eval. This gives 128 repos across six categories: data management (52), system tools (24), web dev (18), code tools (15), ML/AI (14), data viz (6).
- **Install:** run **SWE-agent itself** on the latest commit for up to 100 steps, asking it to install the repo and run the tests. So the agent bootstraps its own training environments.
- **Human check:** a person reads the agent's trajectory and pulls out the correct install steps (~7 min/repo). They require that more than 80% of existing tests pass, then bake a Docker image.
- **Test-output parser:** ~1 min/repo, because pytest parsers can be reused.

Total human labor for the whole dataset: **about 20 hours for one author**. Total dollar cost: **$1,360** ($1,000 bugs, $160 auto-install, $200 issue text for 10k bugs).

### 3.2 Four ways to make bugs

Every strategy outputs a `.diff` candidate. Their design criteria for a strategy were: codebase-agnostic, reliably breaks tests, and controllable through parameters.

**(a) LM Generation** (model: o3-mini). Use Python's `ast` to list every function and class, skipping test directories. Two variants:

- **LM Modify:** show the LM a working function and ask it to add a subtle logical bug. The system prompt casts the model as "a software developer doing chaos monkey testing." Each call shows 3 randomly chosen bug hints out of 9 (wrong calculation order, off-by-one, swallowed exceptions, wrong defaults, and so on). The rules: no syntax errors, don't change the signature, and **no comments marking the bug**. They found that without that last rule the LM leaves comments pointing right at the bug.
- **LM Rewrite:** delete the function body, keep the signature and docstring, give the LM the rest of the file, and ask it to *implement* the function. The prompt never asks for a bug. Any bug is an honest mistake from re-implementing the code, which is why these bugs look more like real ones.

**(b) Procedural Modification** (costs nothing, no LM). Parse the function to an AST, apply a fixed transformation, then turn it back into source code. There are 13 transforms in four groups:

| Group | Transforms |
|---|---|
| Class | Remove methods (and their references), remove a base class, shuffle method order |
| Control flow | Invert if/else bodies, shuffle lines |
| Expressions | ±1 on a numeric constant, break chains (remove operators/operands), swap operands, change an operator (+ → −) |
| Removal | Remove loops, conditionals, assignments, or try/with wrappers |

Each transform comes with filter criteria (for example, "has a conditional," or complexity inside a min/max range). Complexity = count of conditionals + loops + boolean ops + exception blocks + comparison ops. The min filter drops trivial getters and setters; the max filter avoids huge monolithic functions. A **likelihood** parameter p controls how aggressive a transform is: with p = 0.5 and "remove conditionals," each conditional in the function is removed independently with probability 0.5. This stops tasks from becoming impossibly broken.

**(c) Combine Bugs.** Strategies (a) and (b) only touch one function each, but real fixes often span several places. So they merge already-validated single-function bugs:

- *Same file* (Algorithm 1): for each file, list the validated bugs that touch it and sample up to `max_combos` (40) combinations of size `num_bugs` ∈ [2, 4]. Apply each combo in turn. If every patch applies cleanly (no merge conflict), save it and re-validate it as one task. Remove every other combo that reuses one of its bugs, so each atomic bug is used only once. Cap at `limit_per_file` = 3.
- *Same module* (Algorithm 2): build a nested dict following the file tree and collapse it to `depth` = 2 (e.g. `sklearn/feature_extraction`), then combine 2-5 bugs per module. Keep only combos that touch **2+ files**. Why modules: 75% of SWE-bench instances that edit 2+ files stay inside one submodule. Depth 2 was chosen because meaningful modules are usually direct subfolders of the source root. Shallower groupings are meaningless; deeper ones kill yield in small repos.

**(d) PR Mirroring (Invert PRs).** Take real merged PRs that touch Python files, and *undo* them against the **current** codebase. Plain `git apply --reverse` fails on most patches because the surrounding code has moved since. So they give an LM (o3-mini, since reasoning models do this well) the PR diff plus the current file, and ask it to rewrite the whole file with the PR's changes reverted. They skip PRs that touch more than 8 files, because no SWE-bench instance editing more than 6 files has ever been solved, so the expert would fail anyway.

A sanity check shows this works: they mirrored 100 SWE-bench django PRs and recovered **92**. **84** of those break exactly the same Fail-to-Pass tests as the originals, and the other 8 break a subset because some tests have since been removed. They also relax two SWE-bench requirements: a PR no longer needs a linked issue (the issue text can be generated) or its own test changes (validation decides whether existing tests break). This recycles far more real history. Their estimate is that SWE-bench itself could be rebuilt with 10x fewer human hours for about $126.

The catch: the rest of the repo is newer than the PR. Line numbers in original issue text may be wrong, and behavior elsewhere may have drifted.

### 3.3 Validation

Apply the candidate, run the test suite, and keep it only if **≥1 previously passing test now fails**. These become the Fail-to-Pass (F2P) tests, and the tests that still pass become Pass-to-Pass (P2P). Candidates that push the test run past **2 minutes** are thrown out. Each surviving bug is pushed as a branch to a mirror repo and converted to the standard SWE-bench instance format, so any existing SWE-bench harness or agent runs on it unchanged.

### 3.4 Writing the issue text

The issue text strongly affects difficulty. A clear "expected vs. observed" description or a repro script changes how easily the agent can localize the bug. The final recipe gives an LM:

- a randomly chosen **SWE-bench Verified issue as a style demonstration**,
- the bug patch,
- the source of one random F2P test,
- the test execution output.

It asks for a realistic GitHub issue with reproduction code, with some notable rules: mimic the demo's style *including its sloppiness* ("if the demonstrations include human flavor text or fluff, your output should also include" it, "even if it conflicts with your default behavior"). Don't explain the fix. Don't name pytest or the failing test. Cost is about 2.54¢ per issue.

## 4. What the dataset looks like

| Strategy | Yield (breaks ≥1 test) | # Instances | Cost/candidate | Median F2P | Median lines edited |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Combine | 96.9% | 10,092 | 0¢ | 15 | 11 |
| LM Modify | 56.0% | 17,887 | 0.38¢ | 4 | 3 |
| LM Rewrite | 35.0% | 4,173 | 3.93¢ | 4 | 24 |
| PR Mirror | 33.8% | 2,344 | 5.53¢ | 3 | 14 |
| Procedural | 40.2% | 15,641 | 0¢ | 7 | 5 |
| **Total** | 50.1% | **50,137** | 2.32¢ | 6 | 5 |

Things worth noticing:

- **Yield is mostly about test coverage.** A candidate "fails" when no test covers the change, or when the change doesn't actually alter behavior. LM Rewrite yields less than LM Modify because Rewrite never asks for a bug; low yield there partly means the LM re-implemented the function *correctly*.
- **Procedural yield varies widely by transform.** Shuffling methods in a class breaks tests only 1.93% of the time, since method order rarely matters in Python. Inverting an if/else breaks them 47.04% of the time.
- **Combine's ~97% yield is expected**, since its inputs are already validated bugs.
- Even PR Mirroring's 13.18% candidate-level yield (appendix table) beats SWE-bench's own 2,294 / 93,139 = **2.46%**.
- On average there are **381 tasks per repo**, and up to 2,277 for pandas.

### 4.1 Difficulty: a learned difficulty rater

To show the tasks are realistic and not trivial, they trained a difficulty classifier:

- **Data:** 1,699 SWE-bench tasks with human time estimates from the SWE-bench Verified annotation effort (<15 min, 15 min-1 hr, 1-4 hr, 4+ hr). The two rare top classes are merged into "1+ hr," giving three classes.
- **Model:** LoRA fine-tune of Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct (Unsloth). Input is the issue plus the gold patch; output is the label. 80/20 split.
- **Accuracy:** 75.3%, and **every error is off by one class** (it never confuses easy with hard).
- **Difficulty score:** map easy/medium/hard to 1/5/9 and average over a dataset.

| Dataset | Score |
|---|---|
| SWE-bench Lite | 3.89 |
| SWE-bench Verified | 3.96 |
| SWE-bench full | 5.01 |
| SWE-gym | 5.62 |
| SWE-bench Multimodal | 6.04 |
| SWE-smith LM Modify | 3.30 |
| SWE-smith Procedural | 3.60 |
| SWE-smith PR Mirror | 4.88 |
| SWE-smith LM Rewrite | 5.27 |
| SWE-smith Combine | 5.72 |

A non-obvious finding: **LM Modify is the easiest strategy even though it explicitly asks for bugs.** Spot checks showed the open-ended "introduce a subtle bug" prompt mostly produces simple variable-swap mistakes (`a=a; b=b` → `a=b; b=a`). Asking an LM to be creatively buggy doesn't produce diverse bugs; it falls back to a narrow set of go-to bugs. Rewrite bugs are harder because they are *unintended*: they are the kind of mistake a competent engineer re-implementing from a docstring would actually make. This fits the broader point that synthetic data looks most natural when the generator isn't trying to make it look a certain way.

---

## 5. Training: rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT)

### 5.1 The recipe

Rejection-sampling fine-tuning (Yuan et al. 2023), set up following SWE-gym (Pan et al. 2024):

1. Pick a subset of SWE-smith tasks.
2. Run **SWE-agent + expert model** (Claude 3.7 Sonnet mostly; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o for comparisons with prior work). Limits are 75 steps and $2 per run.
3. Record the full trajectories and **keep only the resolved ones** (F2P tests now pass and P2P tests still pass).
4. Supervised fine-tune the student (Qwen 2.5 Coder Instruct 7B / 32B) on those trajectories.
5. Evaluate the student inside the same SWE-agent scaffold at temperature 0, with 75 steps.

In loss terms this is ordinary next-token SFT on a filtered set. For a trajectory τ = (x, a₁, o₁, a₂, o₂, …, a_T), where x is the task prompt, aₜ is the model's (thought, action) turn, and oₜ is the environment observation:

L(θ) = − Σ_{τ ∈ D_resolved} Σ_{t} log π_θ(aₜ | x, a₁, o₁, …, a_{t−1}, o_{t−1})

- π_θ is the student policy (Qwen).
- The sum over t runs only over **assistant turns**; observations oₜ are context, not targets (standard multi-turn agent SFT).
- **D_resolved** is the rejection step: a trajectory enters the dataset only if its final patch passes the tests. Equivalently, this is SFT weighted by a binary reward r(τ) ∈ {0, 1}, the degenerate "filtered behavior cloning" case of policy gradient. There's no negative signal: failed trajectories get weight 0, not a penalty.

**Hyperparameters:** full-parameter fine-tuning with torchtune, LR 5e-5, up to 3 epochs, **32,768-token max context**, 2-8 H100s on Modal. Trajectories average **58 turns (~29 actions)**, which is why the long context matters.

**The agent-computer interface (ACI)** has three tools: `bash`, `str_replace_editor` (view/create/edit files), and `submit`. Each turn is a ReAct-style (thought, action) pair.

### 5.2 Curating the final 5,016 trajectories

- Ablation runs produced 5,105 successful trajectories.
- PR Mirror and LM Rewrite tasks gave the best training signal (Section 6), so they ran the expert on *all* tasks of those two types, reaching 6,457 successful trajectories.
- In total they attempted **8,686 unique tasks (17.3% of the dataset)** in **17,906 attempts**, so the expert's resolve rate was only **36%**. This is a strong sign that the tasks are not trivial: even the state-of-the-art agent solves about a third.
- **Cap of 3 trajectories per task.** This follows SWE-gym's observation that "easy" tasks the expert solves over and over flood the dataset and **hurt** the student, a bias toward easy data. After the cap: **5,016**.

Final mix: PR Mirror 1,848 · LM Rewrite 1,532 · Procedural 1,495 · Combine-file 123 · LM Modify 11 · Combine-module 7. The mix deliberately leaves out the easy LM Modify tasks. The data spans 123 repos, with ≥10 trajectories from 91 of them. The top repos are moto (378), pandas (320), conan (243), pydantic (209), dvc (181), and dask (139).

### 5.3 Main result

**SWE-agent-LM-32B: 40.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified** (up from the base Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B's ~6.8%, the "+33.4" in the paper), plus 30.7% on Lite. **SWE-agent-LM-7B: 15.2% Verified.** At the time this was the best open-weight result without test-time scaling or verifiers. For reference, R2E-Gym-32B scored 34.4% and SWE-gym-32B 20.6% in the table, both on OpenHands.

Important caveats on the headline number:

- Pass@1 is averaged over **6 runs**. Pass@k climbs to roughly **55% at k = 6** (Fig. 22), so there's a lot of headroom for a verifier or best-of-k selection, which they left out on purpose. R2E-Gym's 51% uses 26 attempts per task plus a verifier, so it isn't comparable.
- **Same-budget comparison:** with only 500 trajectories (from Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o experts, matching the prior papers' setup), they reach **28.2%**, which is +8.2 over SWE-gym and +0.7 over R2E-Gym. So at small scale the data *quality* is only on par with R2E-Gym. The big gain comes from **scale plus a stronger expert (3.7 Sonnet)**, which their pipeline makes affordable.
- **Scaling:** Fig. 1 shows performance rising with trajectory count (100 → 5k trajectories), roughly log-linearly.
- **RFT beats unfiltered SFT:** training on randomly sampled trajectories (both successes and failures) is clearly worse at every data size from 100 to 1.6k (Fig. 23). At 1.6k trajectories: 33.4 with filtering vs. 27.8 without.

---

## 6. Ablations: what actually matters in the data

All ablations use Claude 3.7 Sonnet as expert, Qwen 2.5 **7B** as student, and SWE-bench Verified as eval. Training size is capped to the smallest successful-trajectory count so the comparison is fair.

**(1) Bug strategy (1,000 tasks each, capped at 507 trajectories):**

| Strategy | Successful trajs | % Resolved |
|---|---|---|
| LM Modify | 802 | 5.7 ± 1.5 |
| LM Rewrite | 507 | 8.8 ± 1.7 |
| Procedural | 745 | 8.6 ± 1.8 |
| PR Mirror | 557 | 9.2 ± 1.7 |

PR Mirror is best, as expected, since it's closest to SWE-bench's real-PR distribution. The surprise is that **zero-cost AST mutations (Procedural) are nearly as good as real PRs**, and LM Rewrite is too. LM Modify falls well behind: easy tasks → easy trajectories → weak training signal. The error bars overlap for the top three, so "PR Mirror is best" is directional.

**(2) Issue text (600 PR Mirror tasks, capped at 259 trajectories):**

| Issue source | Successful trajs | % Resolved |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed templates | 259 (fewest) | 6.4 ± 1.5 |
| F2P test code + logs | 390 (most) | 7.3 ± 1.9 |
| LM-generated | 328 | 7.7 ± 1.5 |
| Original human issue | 319 | 7.8 ± 1.8 |

LM-generated issues are statistically indistinguishable from real ones as training signal, so the ~70% of PRs without a linked issue, and all synthetic bugs, can be used.

Two useful mechanisms:

- **Templates make the behavior uniform.** Expert trajectories on template issues have **31% fewer unique actions** (379 vs 550). The student learns a narrower set of behaviors.
- **Leaking the test hurts the student in a subtle way.** Giving the F2P test in the issue makes the *expert* succeed more often, but the *student* then learns to **skip writing a reproduction script**, since the test already reproduces the bug. On SWE-bench Verified, where real issues have no attached test, the LM-issue student writes a repro in 379/500 runs, while the test-issue student does so in only 127/500, a **66% drop**. The info that makes training tasks easier removes a skill the eval needs. This is a clean example of train/test mismatch in *task framing*, not just in data content.

**(3) Difficulty ≠ training value.** Expert resolve rates on easy/medium/hard subsets are 58.6% / 41.0% / 17.0%, so difficulty clearly predicts solvability. But SFT sets of 500 trajectories at difficulty scores 2/4/6/8 give **12.4 / 10.8 / 13.6 / 12.2%**, with no clear trend. Harder training data is **not** automatically better. (This conflicts a bit with the per-task cap motivated by "easy data hurts"; the resolution seems to be that *duplicated* easy trajectories hurt, while the difficulty level itself matters less.)

**(4) Repo diversity helps, roughly logarithmically.** With 700 Procedural trajectories sampled from 4 / 25 / 50 / 100 repos, the 7B scores rise from ~10.3% → 11.5% → 12.9% → 15.1%. Each doubling of repos gives a roughly constant gain. Diversity across codebases is an independent axis from task count.

**(5) Repo specialization is cheap and barely hurts generalization.** Target: the 22 SymPy tasks in SWE-bench Verified created after Jan 1, 2022. They check out SymPy just before that cutoff (so no leakage), generate 1,276 Procedural tasks, and collect 700 trajectories.

- 7B trained on SymPy only vs. 7B trained on 100 repos: **21.2% vs 13.6%** on SymPy, with a small loss on the rest of Verified.
- SWE-agent-LM-32B + an extra SymPy stage: **42.4% vs 33.3%** on SymPy, and on Verified-minus-SymPy 38.3% vs 40.2%. (The 7B pair on Verified-minus-SymPy: 14.0% vs 15.3%.)

This is the most practically important result for companies: **you can point SWE-smith at your own private repo and train an agent specialized to it**, gaining ~9 points on that repo while losing ~2 elsewhere.

---

## 7. How the trained agent behaves and fails

**Efficiency.** Resolved runs average 24.9 steps (student) vs 29.1 (Claude 3.7). On tasks both solve, it's 24.8 vs 25.6, nearly the same once you control for difficulty. The student can also stay on track in long runs: 31 tasks were solved after 40+ steps. When the student submits on its own (not cut off by limits), its patches are correct **60%** of the time vs **63%** for Claude, so it's well calibrated about when it's done.

**Repetition is the signature failure.** More than **25%** of student trajectories contain a repeated sequence of **≥10** identical base commands, vs **<4%** for Claude. **73%** of the longest repeated runs are `str_replace_editor view`: the model scrolls through a file chunk by chunk instead of using `grep` or `find`. A repeated run of length 10 means an **89% chance of failure**.

**Most failures come from hitting the budget, not from wrong answers.** 53% of the student's failures hit a cost or step limit, often **before any source file was edited**. That puts them in the "stuck at localization" or "stuck at reproduction" categories. So the dominant failure mode is **localization**: finding where the bug lives. Their failure categories (Fig. 26): error / context exceeded / stuck-localizing / stuck-reproducing / incorrect-localization / incorrect-edit, where "localization correct" means the patch touches every file the gold patch touches.

**The scaffold fix doesn't help, and why that's interesting.** They added warnings after 4 repeated `view` calls (or 6 of any other command), telling the model to use grep or find. Then they forced resampling (up to 10 times) at 6 or 8 repeats, and injected messages or raised the temperature at 7 or 9. Repetition dropped a lot (Fig. 27), **but resolve rate fell slightly to 38.4%** (192/500). Their reading: **repetition is a symptom, not a cause**. The model loops *because* it's lost on an out-of-distribution or hard task, and breaking the loop doesn't make it un-lost. This is a useful caution against symptom-level agent fixes. Compare the resampling-as-control idea in [[2504.10374 - Ctrl-Z - Controlling AI Agents via Resampling]] / [[resampling-for-agent-control]]: there, resampling is used to *avoid suspicious actions*, a safety goal. Here, resampling to avoid *repetitive* actions doesn't add capability.

**Cost/turn statistics are misleading.** Most failures end at the limit, so average cost and step counts mostly reflect the chosen limit (Fig. 24). Any single "cost per instance" figure for this model is an artifact of how it was configured.

---

## 8. Generalization beyond Python: a clear negative result

They introduce **SWE-bench Multilingual**: 300 tasks from 42 repos in 9 languages (JS, TS, C, C++, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby, Rust), built with SWE-bench's method by a single author, and filtered for underspecified issues the way Verified was. Median 1 F2P test, ~48 lines edited.

| Model | Multilingual |
|---|---|
| Claude 3.7 Sonnet | 43% |
| SWE-agent-LM-32B | **8.4%** |
| Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B (base) | 6.5% |

Python-only RFT **doesn't transfer**. The student got better at the multi-turn *agentic* loop but writes Python-flavored syntax into non-Python files. So what was learned is a mix of general agent skill and Python habits, and the Python habits win when the language changes. The authors present this as motivation (the SWE-smith method, especially the LM-based strategies, should carry over to other languages). Still, it is a real limitation: 40% on Verified mostly reflects in-distribution skill.

---

## 9. What SWE-smith is *not* for: evaluation

Appendix C.2 is candid about this:

- **No hidden tests.** The F2P tests are *in the repo* when the agent runs, so an agent could in principle find and read them. That's fine for training data, but disqualifying for a benchmark.
- **Issue text isn't checked** for underspecification or solution leakage, the two things SWE-bench Verified's human pass was designed to catch.
- **Realism isn't established.** Nobody has checked how closely synthetic bugs match real bugs in distribution.

There's also a notable **"bug coverage"** statistic. On flask, SWE-bench's 11 tasks break only 15 of 207 tests (**7.25%**), while SWE-smith's 267 tasks break 422 of 474 (**89%**). Their explanation is interesting: in real development, most tests are written alongside *working* code to protect behavior that is already correct. Well-maintained repos rarely merge commits that break those tests, so real PR history exercises only a small part of the test suite. Synthetic breakage covers the rest. That's a real advantage for training coverage, and also a reason synthetic bugs differ from the real bug distribution: real bugs cluster where the tests *didn't* catch them.

---

## 10. What's interesting / non-obvious

1. **Using execution as a bug filter.** Running the tests is both the check on solutions and the check on whether a bug is real. It's simple, and it removes almost all the human curation.
2. **One environment per repo instead of per task.** This single choice cuts storage by roughly 500x and removes the most expensive human step (version-specific install specs).
3. **Reversing real PRs against today's code** with a reasoning LM, instead of rebuilding old environments. It also relaxes SWE-bench's "linked issue + test changes" filter, which recycles much more real history.
4. **Deliberately buggy prompts produce boring bugs.** Asking for bugs gives easy, repetitive variable swaps. Asking for a correct re-implementation gives harder, more realistic mistakes.
5. **Giving the student more information made it worse.** Leaking the failing test raised expert success but taught the student to skip reproduction.
6. **Task difficulty didn't predict how useful the data was.** Repo diversity and bug type mattered more.
7. **Cheap AST mutations nearly match real PRs as training data.** This suggests the *agentic procedure* (explore, localize, reproduce, edit, verify) is most of what gets learned, not the realism of any particular bug.
8. **The agent bootstraps its own environments.** SWE-agent installs the repos that SWE-agent-LM trains on.

---

## 11. Limitations (as they actually appear)

- **Python only.** Bug generation relies on Python's `ast`, and the negative Multilingual result shows the learned skill doesn't transfer across languages.
- **SFT/RFT only, no RL.** They explicitly leave RL out for budget reasons. The binary test reward is ready-made for online RL (GRPO/PPO), but they don't use it here. Later work does: the dataset became a standard RL environment pool.
- **Some human work remains.** About 8 minutes per repo for checking install steps and writing the test parser. Full automation is future work.
- **Out-of-sync PR mirrors.** The rest of the repo is newer than the reversed PR, so behavior and line references may drift.
- **Exposed tests and ungated issue text** make the data unusable for evaluation as-is.
- **Distillation ceiling.** The student learns only from Claude 3.7's successes, so it's bounded by what the expert can solve (36% of attempted tasks), and the hardest tasks contribute no signal.
- **The headline number depends on a strong closed expert.** At matched small scale with weaker experts, the gain over R2E-Gym is only +0.7.

---

## 12. Company angle: what this says about how the SWE-bench group (and anyone building SWE-agent data) works

This paper is the clearest public write-up of the **"environments as the product"** philosophy that SWE-agent/SWE-bench researchers carry into industry, and that data and RL-environment companies sell:

- **Environments first, tasks second, trajectories third.** The unit of value is an executable repo with a solid test suite. Tasks are cheap to produce once it exists, and trajectories follow from tasks plus a strong model.
- **Verification is the moat.** Everything depends on having an automatic, execution-based check (F2P/P2P). Any company building agent training data or RL environments competes on how cheaply it can make *verifiable* tasks at scale. This is the same logic as [[benchmarks-repurposed-as-training-environments]]: SWE-smith converts the SWE-bench *evaluation* format into a *training* data factory.
- **Rejection sampling from a frontier model as the default bootstrap.** Distill Claude's successful trajectories into an open model first; RL later. The 3-per-task cap is a small, reusable curation rule worth remembering.
- **Per-customer specialization is the commercial pitch.** The SymPy result (+9 points on the target repo, −2 general) is exactly the "point it at your codebase" offering enterprises want. Pre-cutoff checkout is the right way to avoid leakage when doing it.
- **Failure analysis vocabulary:** "stuck at localization," repetitive `view` loops, and cost-limit terminations are the diagnostics to use when evaluating any coding agent. Compare the ML-engineering failure taxonomy in [[llm-agent-failure-modes-in-ml-engineering]] and trace-level issue localization in [[2505.08638 - TRAIL Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization]].
- **Watch for test leakage and overfitting.** Tests visible in the repo during training are the same hazard as [[validation-test-overfitting-in-agent-search]]. An agent trained with RL on SWE-smith tasks could learn to read or special-case the F2P tests. This is a reward-hacking surface to guard against when moving from RFT to RL.

## 13. Connections

- [[2509.02547 - The Landscape of Agentic Reinforcement Learning for LLMs]]: SWE-smith is one of the main open *data/environment* sources feeding agentic RL for coding. This paper's RFT is the supervised precursor to the RL step the survey covers.
- [[2504.20073 - RAGEN StarPO Multi-Turn Agent RL]]: multi-turn agent RL. SWE-smith's repetitive-action collapse looks like the multi-turn degeneration RAGEN studies, but here it appears under SFT alone.
- [[2505.10978 - GiGPO Group-in-Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training]]: step-level credit assignment for long-horizon agents, relevant because SWE-smith trajectories are ~29 actions long with only a binary terminal reward.
- [[distillation-to-single-step-policies]]: RFT here is behavior cloning of a stronger policy filtered by outcome.
- [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]]: another benchmark where execution-based state checks define success. Contrast its user-simulation dimension, which SWE-smith lacks.
